Error handling and retries

The practical integration policy for CALIBER failures: classify them correctly, use waiters where available, and retry only what is actually safe to retry.

Use this page when you need the practical integration policy for failures: which problems are auth or scope issues, which are transient, and when to use waiters instead of building your own polling loop.

1. Classify the failure before retrying#

Start by separating:

  • auth or permission failures
  • wrong-project or wrong-scope failures
  • request-shape or validation failures
  • transient transport or dependency failures

Retrying the first three classes usually only creates noise.

On the wire the classes map to statuses like this:

StatusUsually means
400request-shape failure; a validation failure carries an errors list of loc, msg and type
401no usable credential
403the token's scope, the caller's project role, a project-bound token naming another project, or (where CSRF is enabled) a missing or stale CSRF token
404the object does not exist, or the caller is not a member of its project
409a state conflict (for example a primary owner that cannot be changed, or a duplicate member)
429rate limited; the response carries Retry-After
503a dependency is down: the database, or MLflow (the message names MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI); GET /readiness says which

Some routes also return a reason_code string beside detail; it is optional, so fall back to detail and the status when it is absent.

POST /jobs/{job_id}/apply is the clearest case. Its refusals are 403 (apply_self_approval, apply_creator_unknown, apply_permission_revoked), 409 (apply_candidate_changed, apply_candidate_unverified) and 503 (apply_busy). Each one changed nothing, so it is safe to call again after the cause is fixed, but only apply_busy is worth retrying as it is: it means that, on PostgreSQL, a database lock was not granted within 5 seconds and nothing was decided. The SDK does not retry a POST on its own, so caliber.jobs.apply(...) raises CaliberServerError with reason_code == "apply_busy" and the caller waits and calls again. The other codes need a person to act (a different account, a restored grant, another evaluation pass). A 500 from Apply (a PostgreSQL deadlock victim or, on SQLite, a busy timeout) carries no code: read the job's status before calling again. The table of codes, the recovery for each and an SDK example are in Apply: refusal catalogue, audit and recovery.

2. Use waiters for long-running operations#

If the product already exposes a waiter or polling contract, use that rather than inventing an uncontrolled sleep loop in your application.

That keeps retry behavior aligned with the documented SDK surface. The SDK waiters poll with a growing interval (2 seconds, times 1.5 each poll, up to 15 seconds), never sleep past your deadline, and raise WaitTimeout when it passes. The default deadline is 900 seconds for runs, jobs, evaluations and Workspace operations, and 600 seconds for tool calibration jobs. A job that stops for a person (candidate_ready) is a stopped state, not a timeout.

What the SDK retries for you#

The SDK retries only GET, HEAD and OPTIONS, on a transport error or a 429, 502, 503 or 504. It makes two retries by default (max_retries), waits 0.5 seconds and then 1 second (backoff_factor doubling per attempt), and uses a numeric Retry-After instead when the server sends one. It never retries a POST, PATCH, PUT or DELETE, because it cannot know whether the first attempt took effect; workflow run submission accepts an idempotency_key so you can retry that one safely yourself. The one replay it does make on a write is a single re-send after a CSRF refusal, once it has fetched a token.

3. Retry safely#

For automated retries:

  • prefer idempotent reads first
  • be careful with writes that can change external state
  • capture request identifiers and final error context
